node.label: Cole Harris
node.date_label: The Seigneurial System in Early Canada 1966 · Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (editor) 1987 · The Resettlement of British Columbia 1997 · ‘Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia’ 1997–98 · Making Native Space 2002 · ‘Revisiting the Native Land Question’ 2003 · ‘How Did Colonialism Dispossess?’ 2004 · A Bounded Land 2020
node.description: A Canadian historical geographer of early Canada and of colonialism in British Columbia. He edited the first volume of the Historical Atlas of Canada (1987), whose preface says it sought 'to emphasize the economic and social circumstances of ordinary life rather than the more usual fare of historical atlases' (as quoted by MacDonald, 1990). From the 1990s he wrote British Columbia's colonization as geographical change. Against the 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era history he set 'epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (1997–98). He explained the reserve system as dispossession: its capacity 'rested on raw firepower', its momentum 'came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods', and its legitimation 'lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery' (2003); in 2004 he argued that the emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'. Reviewers found few Native voices in the work: Tina Loo (1998) saw Native peoples 'emerge as victims' in The Resettlement of British Columbia, and Val Napoleon (2004) wrote that Making Native Space 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history' and that Harris 'should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices' where history gave way to proposals for the future.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Cole Harris (R. Cole Harris, 1936–2022); The Seigneurial System in Early Canada (1966); 'Theory and Synthesis in Historical Geography' (Canadian Geographer, 1971); 'The Simplification of Europe Overseas' (Annals of the AAG, 1977); 'The Historical Mind and the Practice of Geography' (1978); ed., with Geoffrey J. Matthews as cartographer and designer, Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1: From the Beginning to 1800 (1987); 'Power, Modernity, and Historical Geography' (Annals of the AAG, 1991); The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change (1997; two chapters with Robert Galois and David Demeritt); 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia' (BC Studies, 1997/98); Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia (2002); 'Revisiting the Native Land Question' (BC Studies forum, 2003, with commentaries by Jo-Anne Fiske and Gordon Gibson and his reply); 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire' (Annals of the AAG, 2004); A Bounded Land: Reflections on Settler Colonialism in Canada (2020). Readings: MacDonald (1990); Loo (1998); Clayton (2003); Fiske (2003); Napoleon (2004); Perry (2016, later reading). Further selected bibliography: The Reluctant Land: Society, Space, and Environment in Canada before Confederation (2008).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14 in open copies. His own words, read: 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia' (BC Studies 115/116, 1997/98, pp. 45–82; pp. 45–47, 56–60, 68–70 and 80–82 read closely, the rest skimmed); 'Revisiting the Native Land Question' with Fiske's and Gibson's commentaries and his reply (BC Studies 138/139, 2003, pp. 137–163, read in full); the abstract of 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess?' (2004), read in the publisher's abstract as recorded by OpenAlex (the article body is closed and unread); the preface of the Historical Atlas of Canada, vol. 1 (1987), known only through MacDonald's quotations. Reception read in full: Graham A. MacDonald on the Atlas (Manitoba History 20, 1990, web text); Tina Loo on The Resettlement of British Columbia (BC Studies 117, 1998, pp. 64–67); Daniel Clayton's guest editorial on Making Native Space (BC Studies 138/139, 2003, pp. 5–11); Val Napoleon on Making Native Space (BC Studies 141, 2004, pp. 114–118). Later reading: Perry's 2016 reply in the BC Studies forum on her Colonial Relations (p. 112). Unread: the books themselves (The Seigneurial System, the Atlas, The Resettlement of British Columbia, Making Native Space, A Bounded Land), the 1977 and 1991 Annals essays (known through Clayton's note), the 1994 Ethnohistory article on smallpox, the Canadian Geographer review symposium on Making Native Space (2003; known through Napoleon's summary), and the Native Studies Review forum 'Appraising Cole Harris' Making Native Space' (16:2, 2005; the copy on the University of Saskatchewan site returned 404). He is not presented as a founder of historical geography or of settler-colonial history: the Atlas was a collective work with a cartographer and many contributors, and the texts read do not cite Wolfe. Contested in period by Loo (1998) and Napoleon (2004) on Native voices and agency, by Fiske (2003) on the symbolic, and by the Canadian Geographer symposium (2003, as Napoleon summarises it). Post-2000 works are dated in labels and text. Canonical-work review (2026-10-24): added titles and dates are selected bibliography, not a complete career or a new reading of the books. Original works, translations, edited collections and posthumous editions are distinguished; earlier argument and source-reading qualifications remain.

incident_edges.relationship: British Columbia's reserve system explained as geographical dispossession: a capacity resting on state-backed force, a momentum from capital and settlers, a legitimation in a discourse of civilization and savagery, and a management by 'disciplinary technologies' of maps, numbers, law and the land system (1997–2004); written in a settler society's terms ('successful settler colonialism', 2003), with no derivation from Wolfe's theory established by the texts checked, and faulted by reviewers for few Native voices
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words. 'Revisiting the Native Land Question', BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 137–151, his précis of Making Native Space, read in full: the reserves comprised 'slightly more than one-third of 1 per cent of provincial land' (p. 137); 'The capacity to dispossess rested on raw firepower authorized, usually, by the administrative superstructure of the state. … The momentum to dispossess came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods' (p. 137); 'The legitimation of dispossession lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery … the implementation of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies among which maps, numbers, and, especially, the common law were essential' (p. 138); 'two very different stories underlie British Columbia. One is about progress and development … It rests, however, on the other basic story about this place, which is about dispossession, loss, marginalization, and the struggle for survival' (p. 140); 'Given the values and benefits associated with successful settler colonialism, many British Columbians will find this an exceedingly difficult commitment' (p. 144, of a politics of difference). The 2004 abstract (publisher's abstract via OpenAlex; article unread) states the same four conclusions: 'the initial ability to dispossess rested primarily on physical power and the supporting infrastructure of the state; the momentum to dispossess derived from the interest of capital in profit and of settlers in forging new livelihoods; the legitimation of and moral justification for dispossession lay in a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery …; and the management of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies of which maps, numbers, law, and the geography of resettlement itself were the most important.' In-period reception. Tina Loo, review of The Resettlement of British Columbia, BC Studies 117 (1998), pp. 64–67, read in full: Harris 'locates the non-Native settlement of British Columbia explicitly in the context of the expansion of European imperial and commercial power' and sees colonization as 'the displacement of Indigenous peoples and the remaking of space that was formerly theirs into an immigrant society' (p. 64); but 'there are very few "Native voices" in it - something Harris himself admits', and Native peoples, 'despite a few examples to the contrary, emerge as victims' (p. 66); in the later chapters 'the connections to colonization … increasingly fade away' and class is not discussed (pp. 66–67); still 'a provocative and important book' (p. 67). Daniel Clayton, BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 5–11, read in full: 'Harris's most political work to date and arguably the most significant contribution to our understanding of colonialism in the province since Robin Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977)' (p. 6). Jo-Anne Fiske, commentary in the 2003 forum (pp. 151–155, read): he 'says little … of how a change in mindset and a marshalling of political will might be achieved', and what he says of the symbolic 'is unsettling in its apparent simplicity' (p. 152); the powers he describes 'did not and cannot exist outside of the symbolic realm' (p. 152). Harris replied: 'I doubt that Jo-Anne Fiske and I have any real disagreement' (p. 161). Val Napoleon (2004): see pe139_harris_rel_07. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: they cite Merivale, Kymlicka and Macklem, not Wolfe, and the books are unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Harris wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later reading, labelled: Perry (BC Studies 190, 2016, p. 112) says her 2001 book read British Columbia 'within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books'. A Bounded Land (2020), with its 'Postscript: The Boundaries of Settler Colonialism', is cited at title level only.

incident_edges.relationship: Colonialism read through its geographies: the land system as a 'spatial discipline' that bounded Native movement, and the reserve line as the 'primal line on the land' of British Columbia (1997–2003), which Clayton (2003) offered as a model of 'colonialism's geographies rather than geography's empire'
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words. 2003 forum précis (p. 138, read): 'From a Native perspective, an even more enveloping discipline may have been imposed by an introduced land system and its associated settlement geography, which, by controlling where they could and could not go, increasingly bounded and channeled their movements.' The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997) is unread; Loo (1998, p. 65, read) quotes it: the land system '[imposing] a spatial discipline with a profound capacity to modify Native life' (p. 101), and by 1881 'Native power over the Lower Mainland and, to a considerable extent, earlier Native lifeworlds had collapsed' (p. 102); Loo: 'According to Harris, in British Columbia disciplinary power rested on the land system (Chapters 3 and 4). To me, this is the heart of Harris's argument … the links between colonization and geographical change are most visible' (p. 65). Making Native Space (2002) is unread; Clayton (2003, read) quotes Harris's aim to tell 'the colonial construction of space in British Columbia' (p. 6, citing pp. xxi, xxviii) and his view that the reserve line 'became, in a sense, the primal line on the land of British Columbia, the one that facilitated or constrained all others' (p. 7); Napoleon (2004, p. 116, read) quotes the reserves 'displayed rather like insects on pins' (p. 271) and their 'fixed place in the Cartesian space of the survey system and in the minds of officials and settlers'. Disciplinary reception (Clayton, a geographer who began working with Harris as a UBC graduate student, p. 6): Harris is 'very much the historian's geographer' (p. 5); the book 'will be more widely read and appreciated for what it says about the spatiality of colonialism, or what Harris sees as colonialism's "geographical core" (xxiv)' (p. 7); he offers '(however unwittingly) a powerful and important programme for a postcolonial historical geography that significantly departs from current critical norms' (p. 7), 'a timely and potent model for the critical appreciation of colonialism's geographies rather than geography's empire' (p. 11), Clayton's contrast with work that 'fixates on the formal disciplinary links between geography and empire' (p. 7). Qualifications: Clayton thinks Harris 'insulate[s]' his historical geography 'from some potentially fruitful comparative lines of inquiry and a fuller digging into theory' (p. 9); the existing spatialhistory row records that the analysis of Merivale and imperial policy 'is not Indigenous testimony'. Distinct from edge 1, which carries the explanation of dispossession in the settler-colonial field; this edge carries the spatial method as historical geography. Compare edge_693 (post → geography, Said in Driver's 'geography's empire').

incident_edges.relationship: The 'cultural enrichment hypothesis' of contact-era British Columbia, as anthropologists and Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977) held it, questioned: it 'needs to be approached very cautiously', since epidemics, violence and depopulation accompanied the fur trade's wealth (1997–98)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words, in period. 'Social Power and Cultural Change in Pre-Colonial British Columbia', BC Studies 115/116 (1997/98), pp. 45–82, read at pp. 45–47, 56–60, 68–70 and 80–82. The position: Fisher, influenced by Wilson Duff's view that the fur trade 'did not destabilize Native life' and by 'his own sharp reaction to the effacement of Native peoples implicit in the "fatal impact" approach', wrote 'a remarkable and influential book — Contact and Conflict — [arguing] that Europeans and Natives met as equals on the Northwest Coast, that contact violence has been considerably exaggerated, and that an infusion of wealth created a brief high point in Northwest Coast culture' (pp. 46–47); 'Fisher's conclusions summarized and extended the prevailing anthropological understanding of the previous generation — a set of assumptions often loosely labelled the cultural enrichment hypothesis, after a phrase first used by Joyce Wike' (p. 47); 'now, twenty years later, new information is available, Native voices have repoliticized issues of land and colonial appropriation, and the intellectual climate has changed' (p. 47). The critique: 'the cultural enrichment hypothesis needs to be approached very cautiously. Crudely applied, it quickly becomes Eurocentric and far too simple. It tends to measure cultural achievement against quantitative and materialistic Western values of accumulation' (p. 80); 'There was no one culture and no fixed datum plane against which to measure cultural enrichment'; 'the enrichment hypothesis ignores too much of what was going on along the Northwest Coast during the contact years. Against enrichment measured by poles, feast goods, and the enhanced authority of some chiefs were epidemics, increased violence, depopulation, and, for many, a drastic loss of cultural and historical memory' (p. 81). Fur-trade power: traders' 'politics of fear — "respect" or "terror" were the traders' common words' (p. 58). Qualifications kept: 'There is good evidence for all of these developments' (p. 80); 'Native people were anything but passive victims of these new circumstances, some of which they had largely made themselves. They drew hard trading bargains' (p. 81); and he calls Fisher's book 'remarkable and influential'. The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997, unread) makes the same case in its first chapters; Loo (1998, p. 65, read) summarises the Hudson's Bay Company as a 'proto-colonial presence' (p. 34) whose rule, 'though founded on fear and violence, relied on symbolic gesture and theatre'. Clayton (2003, p. 6, read) measures Making Native Space against Contact and Conflict. No reply by Fisher was checked. Scope: a critique of one interpretation of early contact, not of the native–newcomer field or of agency-centred work as such; edge_868 carries the Indigenous critiques of the field's framing.

incident_edges.relationship: Colonial-discourse studies criticised for an emphasis on culture that 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'; he proposed explaining 'colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized' instead, while allowing that 'several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights' (2004)
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words. Abstract of 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire', Annals of the Association of American Geographers 94:1 (2004), pp. 165–182 (publisher's abstract, read via OpenAlex; article body closed and unread): 'The emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism tends to obscure other forms of colonial power while making it impossible to contextualize the cultural argument and assess its salience. Rather than focusing on texts, systems of signification, and procedures of knowledge generation, as the colonial discourse literature is wont to do, a fuller understanding of colonial powers is achieved by explaining colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized. In so doing, the issue of power is not prejudged'; it ends 'Although no one body of theory explains colonial power, several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights.' The 2003 précis (BC Studies, pp. 137–138, read) gives culture one of four roles, the legitimation of dispossession. Qualifications: he uses the literature he criticises. In 1997–98 (p. 59 n. 39, read) he cites Said's Orientalism as 'The original and most influential discussion' of the European categories of civilized and savage; Napoleon (2004, p. 114, read) finds Making Native Space 'Informed by Frantz Fanon, Edward Said, Michel Foucault, and E.P. Thompson'. Clayton's reading, labelled as his (2003, read): Harris is 'neither a close student of the imperial imagination nor a slavish follower of the powerful postcolonial theories' (p. 8, Clayton's paraphrase); his findings fuel 'his suspicion of an international postcolonial literature that, in his view, tends to overplay the hands of culture and discourse relative to other forms of power' (pp. 8–9, citing the 2004 essay as forthcoming); yet he 'favours (again however unwittingly) a certain postcolonial narrative' (p. 9) and 'has absorbed a body of ideas about the ascriptive power of colonial discourse … that were initially advanced by Said' (p. 10). No reply from a postcolonial critic was checked.
incident_edges.map_label: Harris: culture overweighted in colonial-discourse studies, 2003–04

incident_edges.relationship: Foucault's sovereign and disciplinary power as Harris's terms for the fur traders' 'politics of fear' and for the colonial land system and its 'disciplinary technologies' (1997–2004), used selectively
incident_edges.evidence_note: His own words. 1997–98 (BC Studies 115/116, p. 58, read): the traders' retaliations 'in public theatres of power' were 'what Michel Foucault called sovereign power, a sporadic, local, and highly visible seizure of property or life', quoting Discipline and Punish (n. 37); he adds that 'In the Cordillera, such power did not validate a discourse of legal rights and property relations, as it did in Europe.' 2003 précis (p. 138, read) and 2004 abstract: the management of dispossession by 'disciplinary technologies'. In-period readers. Loo (1998, read): the HBC's power was 'what Harris, following Michel Foucault, calls "sovereign power"', and 'the resettlement of British Columbia turned on "disciplinary power,"' which in British Columbia 'rested on the land system' (p. 65); the book 'is shaped by his reading of a diverse and complex international theoretical literature on power' (p. 64). Napoleon (2004, p. 114, read) names Foucault with Fanon, Said and Thompson. Qualification: Clayton (2003, p. 9, read) reports that Harris never '"lets theory loose" in British Columbia, as he puts it (xvii)'. The 1991 'Power, Modernity, and Historical Geography' (Annals of the AAG), which Clayton lists among his methodological essays (p. 6 n. 3), is unread.

incident_edges.relationship: Val Napoleon's review of Making Native Space (2004): the book 'recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history', its proposals needed 'contemporary Aboriginal voices', and grounding Aboriginal rights in 'difference' is problematic, since Aboriginal peoples 'still have a special place in Canada' whether or not they are 'the same as everyone else'
incident_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Val Napoleon's review (BC Studies 141, Spring 2004, pp. 114–118, read in full), not a verdict of the Indigenous history field, whose roster also lists Harris as a historian. Her criticisms: 'Harris recreates, from a settler perspective, BC history as it unfolded for roughly a century' (p. 115); Part 4, 'Land and Livelihood', is 'somewhat incongruous with the rest of the book' because there he moves from the archival record to argument (p. 117); the politics of difference is 'nonetheless problematic' (p. 117), and 'Speaking as a First Nations person, I do not believe that it matters whether Aboriginal people are the same as everyone else; we still have a special place in Canada' (p. 117); 'In my view, where historical enquiry gives way to thought about the future, Harris should have incorporated contemporary Aboriginal voices into his discussion … It is from within the experience of this conflicted and contradictory milieu that strategies for future change must be developed and tested, not from without' (p. 117); he does not address 'the structural economic problems that small communities are encountering' (p. 115). Her praise, kept: the book gave her 'a much more textured, dynamic, and human sense of BC history' (p. 116); 'What I appreciate most … is Harris's argument that the colonial approach to land was less about legal or moral principles than about the varying self-interests of the colonizers' (p. 117); it is 'a valuable resource for both Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal peoples', and she has 'recommended the book to people from several different Aboriginal communities' (p. 118). She also summarises, without quotation, the Canadian Geographer review symposium of five geographers (47:1, 2003, unread here): they suggested that Harris had '(1) appropriated the voices of patriarchy and of the colonizer' and '(5) insufficiently considered Aboriginal resistance to the reserve allocation system' (pp. 114–115), and Harris replied that 'A book … can only do so much' and 'remains unconvinced that the basic settler attitudes were gendered' (p. 115, her words). Loo (1998, p. 66, read) had made the related point that 'there are very few "Native voices"' in the 1997 book (edge 1). A field-to-person critique naming its proxy, the pattern used for quebec_historiography → fernand_ouellet.

incident_edges.relationship: Wolfe took from Harris the sentence that 'the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus' when capital's interest in uncluttered access to land is combined with settlers' interest in land as livelihood (2004, quoted 2006): a use as evidence, moderate
incident_edges.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), third section and note 36, quoting Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess?" (2004), p. 179: "Combine capital's interest in uncluttered access to land and settlers' interest in land as livelihood, and the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus." Englert 2020 (read) also uses Harris 2004, p. 172, against Wolfe. The direction matters for edge_1014, which found no derivation of Harris from Wolfe: the citation runs the other way. A single quotation; influence in the sense of a use as evidence, as for locB_rel_26 in revision 1.152. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

incident_edges.relationship: Coulthard takes from Canadian historians and geographers, citing Harris, that after the waves of settlement (1860–1914) colonial development 'required first and foremost land, and only secondarily' Indigenous labour: the historical ground of 'dispossession, not proletarianization' (2009)
incident_edges.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), p. 18 (read): 'It is now generally acknowledged among Canadian historians and political economists' that Native labour became 'increasingly (although by no means entirely) superfluous'; n. 48 cites Harris, 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess?' (2004), p. 167, for the land-over-labour claim; n. 47 also cites Lutz, Makuk (2008), 'On the importance of Native labour'. Restated in the conclusion, p. 215: 'as most political economists and historians have now recognized'. A use, not a critique. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Region questioned as a unit of analysis: regional history's strengths and weaknesses weighed (1977), and regions recast as provinces, 'a concept whose time has gone' (1983)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Cook's own review essays in Acadiensis, read in full. 'The Burden of Regionalism' (7:1, Autumn 1977, pp. 110–115), reviewing Bercuson's Canada and the Burden of Unity among other books, notes 'the tendency to see regionalism as a virtue of Canadian life rather than an obstacle to Canadian unity' (p. 110). Bercuson's contributors assume 'that Canadian history is best understood from a regional perspective' (p. 112), but 'neither he nor anyone else in the book attempts to define the term' (p. 114); 'the “regional” approach to Canadian history, and to its discontents, has both strengths and weaknesses. The whole may not be greater than the parts, but it is at least the sum of them' (p. 115). 'Regionalism Unmasked' (13:1, Autumn 1983, pp. 137–142), reviewing L. D. McCann's Heartland and Hinterland (1982): 'I have begun to doubt seriously the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions, though regionalism as a rationalization of certain interests may have some reality' (p. 140); McCann's definition of region 'applies at least as well, and perhaps better, to a province as to a region. So why not call a region what it really is — a province' (p. 140); with Cole Harris's chapter, the book 'can really lead to no other conclusion than that, as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone' (p. 141). He qualifies this: 'Stripped of its rhetoric there remains with the regional approach, especially as practised by historical geographers, a legitimate preoccupation with some profoundly important aspects of our history: class, sex, family, ethnicity, for example' (p. 141), and he calls Wynn's Maritimes chapter 'the finest section of the book' (p. 138). In-period response: Buckner (2000, pp. 8–10) cites both reviews, though he dates the first 1974 and renders 'whose time is gone' where the 1983 page reads 'has gone'. He calls the fragmentation charge 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8) and holds that the Atlantic Provinces 'had legitimate grievances within Confederation' (p. 10), adding that he was 'initially ... as skeptical as Cook' (p. 10). The critique targets the regional framework and heartland–hinterland synthesis, not regional research as such.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gender and race in the making of a would-be white settler colony: British Columbia, 1849–71, where colonization and immigration were meant to produce a white, respectable society among a majority of Aboriginal people and failed to do so (2001), which she said was inspired by an international literature on gender and colonialism (no derivation from Wolfe's settler-colonial theory is established by the texts checked); later described by her as a comparative settler-colonial argument (2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History', BC Studies 132 (2001/02), pp. 57–64, read in full: On the Edge of Empire 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism. That through reading about imperialism elsewhere I came to see imperialism where I was is a suggestive comment on the convenient erasure of dispossession' (p. 58; the sentence ends 'settler consciousness' without a connecting word); 'The most remarkable pattern of silence probably concerns Aboriginal peoples' (p. 61). The 1995 essay (pp. 42–43, read) calls British Columbia 'a racially divided one controlled by a minority white population constantly engaged in a process of colonization' (p. 42). The book is unread; reviewers quote it: 'In contemporary newspapers and conversations, White British Columbians often long for the days when our society was unquestionably British … When we do so we long for a fiction of our own invention' (p. 201, as quoted by Carter, p. 117). In-period reviews. Sarah Carter, BC Studies 136 (2002/03), pp. 117–119, read in full: 'British Columbia fits within a broader context of European colonialism in that it was a settler colony where dispossesion [sic] of the indigenous societies and resettlement by a newcomer population were intertwined. While this is imperial history, it is not an example of the triumph of imperialism as in this era Aboriginal peoples remained demographically dominant and socially central' (p. 117); but 'The theme of the "social centrality and political agency" of the Aboriginal peoples of British Columbia could have been further developed' (p. 119). Myra Rutherdale, Labour/Le Travail 50 (2002), pp. 324–326, read in full: Perry shows 'how colonization and immigration worked in tandem in an attempt to create a White colony, while at the same time deliberately marginalizing the majority of the population, the Aboriginal peoples' (p. 325). Paul Orlowski, Left History 8:1 (2002), pp. 119–122, read in full: 'I found Perry's rendering of First Nations resistance to be lacking throughout much of the work, their portrayal emphasizing passivity rather than agency' (p. 121). Her own caution (1995, p. 43): 'my analysis minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: the 2001 essay cites Said, McClintock, Burton and Chakrabarty, not Wolfe, and the book is unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Perry wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later readings, labelled: in the BC Studies 190 forum (2016) she says the 2001 book 'makes the argument that British Columbia's history is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books' (p. 112); Tony Ballantyne (2016, pp. 104–105) reads Colonial Relations (2015) as 'a salutary reminder of the limitations of work that follows Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini in understanding "settler colonialism" as a fundamentally eliminationist project'.

sources.title: P. A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited: Regionalism and Nationalism in Canadian History," Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 4–15.
sources.citation: P. A. Buckner, "'Limited Identities' Revisited: Regionalism and Nationalism in Canadian History," Acadiensis 30, no. 1 (Autumn 2000): 4–15.

verification.note: Pages 4–5 read: Cook coined "limited identities" (1967) and Careless popularized it (1969); before the 1960s historians emphasized "the economic and political unity of Canada as it evolved from a colony into an independent nation-state"; "liberal nationalists such as A.R.M. Lower and Frank Underhill, and … conservative nationalists such as Donald Creighton and C.P. Stacey"; the approach was "similar to that of the consensus school in the United States"; Cook and Careless embraced limited identities partly in response to Quebec separatism; Atlantic historians espoused it for other reasons. The rest of the essay is unread. Paragraphs 4–6 read on 2026-10-12 after the Sol review: Ken Windsor "initiated and eloquently defended the creation of a journal"; David Earl showed it would be viable; Buckner "agreed to become the editor"; the title was revived from David Russell Jack's journal (1901–08). Checked against: UNB Libraries Acadiensis article page and PDF (citation line on p. 4). Addendum 2026-10-14: Re-read for the 1.135 Ramsay Cook entry (UNB PDF, pp. 4–5, 8–10, 12, notes 1–5 and 13–20). Quoted: Cook's 1967 sentence on 'the regional, ethnic and class identities that we do have' and Careless's 'limited identities of region, culture and class referred to by Professor Cook' (p. 4); Cook's 1970 essay, 'a strait-jacket identity' (p. 4) and 'Nationalism by nature tends strongly to centralism and uniformity' (p. 5, quoting The Maple Leaf Forever p. 213); Cook and Careless embraced limited identities partly in response to Quebec separatism; Atlantic historians 'eagerly espoused' it with other motives (p. 5); Cook 'mockingly' recalled being made an honorary Maritimer; fragmentation 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region'; in 1977 Cook 'warned regional historians of the danger of ignoring the “national experience”'; 1983, 'regionalism' 'a concept whose time is gone' (the 1983 page reads 'has gone'); 1995, the phrase 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8); Careless 1980 and Bliss, Granatstein and Owram on limited identities having gone too far (p. 9); Atlantic 'legitimate grievances within Confederation' (p. 10); the additive model of identity 'nonsensical'; 'All identities are socially constructed' (p. 12). Note 15 dates 'The Burden of Regionalism' Autumn 1974; the review is of 1977 books and its OJS record is 1977. Note 15 also gives Cook's 2000 CHR essay as 81:2 (June 2000), pp. 260–65. [careless draft: Pages 4–10 read for the 1.135 person entry (Érudit PDF). Added: Cook 1995 on the phrase, 'usually attributed to Maurice Careless and I have decided that he is welcome to it!' (p. 8, n. 15); Careless 'too had come to the conclusion that the search for limited identities had gone too far' (pp. 8–9, citing Manitoba History, cited as 1980, p. 7); the same point made 'somewhat crudely, by Michael Bliss and Jack Granatstein and with greater sophistication by Doug Owram' (p. 9); the 'so-called fragmentation' as 'patently absurd, at least when applied to the Atlantic region' (p. 8); regionalism treated, 'as Careless and Granatstein seem to believe', as 'a construct designed to justify the dismantling of the Canadian state' (p. 10); the 1969 article reprinted in Careless at Work (1990), pp. 281–91 (p. 4, n. 2).] Addendum 2026-10-26: Dedicated Owram review: fresh official full-text HTML, especially numbered paragraphs 10–15 (printed 9–12) and notes 18/19/22. Buckner quotes Owram’s 1997 Narrow Circles and 1989 Ontario argument, distinguishes his two claims, disputes the specialization/region equation and partial national-law claims, and agrees with the concluding interplay of identities. Both Owram originals remain unread; this is explicit named scholarly mediation, not a new reading of those essays. Separately scoped dedicated-person reading: Actual UNB public PDF freshly retrieved. Selected 8–10 and notes 13–20 read for Granatstein/Owram comparison and Buckner’s particular criticism; selected 6 read to disambiguate Buckner/Windsor/Earl’s Creighton influence from any Granatstein debt. Existing earlier reading/date/source qualifications retained; Granatstein 1998/Owram 1997 originals unread.

sources.scope_note: Characterizes the national tradition and the origin of limited identities.

sources.title: Ramsay Cook, “The Burden of Regionalism,” Acadiensis 7, no. 1 (Autumn 1977): 110–115 (review essay).
sources.citation: Ramsay Cook, “The Burden of Regionalism,” Acadiensis 7:1 (Autumn 1977): 110–115. Review of Mildred Schwartz, Politics and Territory (1974); David Cameron, Nationalism, Self-Determination and the Quebec Question (1974); and David Bercuson, ed., Canada and the Burden of Unity (1977).

verification.note: Read in full in the UNB Libraries Acadiensis PDF (OJS article 11456; the OJS record misspells the author 'Ramsey Cook'; the review is signed RAMSAY COOK, p. 115; running heads give pp. 111–115, and the first page is 110 per the OJS record). Volume and issue follow Buckner 2000 n. 15 (VII, 1); Buckner dates it Autumn 1974, but the OJS record and the 1977 books reviewed, Bercuson 1977 and Alexander's Canadian Forum letter of September 1977 (n. 1), date it 1977. Quoted: 'the tendency to see regionalism as a virtue of Canadian life rather than an obstacle to Canadian unity'; the Laurentian view hardly acceptable 'as “national”' in the Fraser, Red or Restigouche valleys, 'a point made long ago by W. L. Morton'; 'And the other nationalist themes fare little better' (p. 110); Bercuson's contributors assume 'that Canadian history is best understood from a regional perspective' (p. 112); no one 'attempts to define the term' (p. 114); the regional approach 'has both strengths and weaknesses. The whole may not be greater than the parts, but it is at least the sum of them' (p. 115). Addendum 2026-10-30: Complete own review 110–115 and its two notes freshly read in the original Acadiensis journal PDF. National versus regional focus, attribution to W. L. Morton, defined-region difficulties, shared benefits and shortcomings retained. Reviewed books, correspondence and underlying documents remain unread.

sources.scope_note: Cook's own in-period review essay on regional history and the Laurentian view.

sources.title: Ramsay Cook, “Regionalism Unmasked,” Acadiensis 13, no. 1 (Autumn 1983): 137–142 (review of L. D. McCann, ed., Heartland and Hinterland: A Geography of Canada, 1982).
sources.citation: Ramsay Cook, “Regionalism Unmasked,” Acadiensis 13:1 (Autumn 1983): 137–142.

verification.note: Read in full in the UNB Libraries Acadiensis PDF (OJS article 12212; OJS author 'Ramsey Cook'; signed RAMSAY COOK, p. 142; running heads pp. 137–142). Volume and issue follow Buckner 2000 n. 15 (XIII, 1, Autumn 1983). The first words of p. 137 ('SINCE THE 19ÔOS') are garbled in the text layer, so the decade is not quoted. Quoted: the 'national' approach 'has come under a destructive barrage of criticism'; Berger's book 'a lengthy epitaph on the headstone of the national school's grave'; Morton's 'Clio in Canada' 'made explicit what had long been implicit in the Innis-Creighton laurentian thesis' (p. 137); Wynn's chapter 'the finest section of the book' (p. 138); 'I have begun to doubt seriously the existence of the phenomena we have for so long called regions'; 'So why not call a region what it really is — a province' (p. 140); 'as a tool of analysis, “regionalism” is a concept whose time has gone'; 'Stripped of its rhetoric ... a legitimate preoccupation with ... class, sex, family, ethnicity' (p. 141). Buckner 2000 (p. 8) quotes the key sentence as 'whose time is gone'; the page reads 'has gone'. Addendum 2026-10-30: Complete own review 137–142 and all eight notes freshly read in the original Acadiensis journal PDF. Berger’s historiographical framing at137 and the specific Cole Harris use138/141 support bounded personal-resource proposals. Graeme Wynn’s chapter receives the strongest chapter praise; his missing full endpoint is held. Cook’s qualified defense of class, sex, family and ethnicity research survives his rejection of regionalism as a general unit. Original chapters and cited books remain unread; the next review beginning on142 is a different signed text.

sources.scope_note: Cook's own in-period critique of region as a unit of analysis.

verification.note: Abstract read: argues that an emphasis on culture in colonial-discourse studies obscures other colonial powers, and explains British Columbia's reserve system as geographical dispossession. The ability to dispossess rested on physical power and the state, its momentum on capital and settlers, and its legitimation on cultural discourse. Addendum 2026-10-14: Abstract re-read verbatim for the 1.139 Cole Harris draft (OpenAlex record of doi:10.1111/j.1467-8306.2004.09401009.x; Crossref has no abstract). It names 'the colonial discourse literature', proposes 'explaining colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized', gives the four conclusions (physical power and the state; capital and settlers; a cultural discourse of civilization and savagery; 'disciplinary technologies of which maps, numbers, law, and the geography of resettlement itself were the most important'), and ends 'Although no one body of theory explains colonial power, several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights.' Article body unread (closed). Addendum 2026-10-23: Wolfe 2006 (read in full) quotes p. 179 approvingly (note 36): "Combine capital's interest in uncluttered access to land and settlers' interest in land as livelihood, and the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus"; Englert 2020 cites p. 172 for Indigenous incorporation into the workforce. The direction of use runs Harris → Wolfe.
